title: The year of advantage—and what comes next
content: Quantum Research Blog The year of advantage—and what comes next IBM Quantum Developer Conference 2026 brings advances in hardware, software, and applications for turning quantum advantage into real-world impact. Date 11 Nov 2026 Authors IBM Quantum Topics Algorithms Community Error Correction & Mitigation Software Systems Share this blog Was this blog post helpful? Yes No Key takeaways: The research community reached quantum advantage in 2026, running computations beyond classical methods with results that can be rigorously verified. IBM Quantum Nighthawk r2, its fastest processor yet, supports accurate circuits with more than 7,500 quantum operations on 120 programmable qubits, and delivers up to 100,000 samples per second, a 25x gain over Heron. Progress toward 100 million operations and IBM Quantum Starling, the fault-tolerant computer IBM plans to deliver in 2029, is backed by detailed plans guiding parallel co-design of memory, l-couplers, decoders, and cryogenics. The directed execution model and new managed workflows on IBM Quantum Functions scale hybrid quantum-classical workloads across billions of samples. New tools—Qiskit Fermions, Qiskit Bosons, optimization mappers—and 39 client projects turn verified advantage into practical applications. Two years ago, we predicted that the first demonstrations of quantum advantage would arrive by the end of 2026, if the quantum and high-performance computing communities worked together. This year, together, we did it . Researchers ran computations beyond purely classical methods, and did so with results that can be rigorously verified. That combination of performance and trust makes this the year of advantage. But advantage is a milestone, not a destination. We’ve shown quantum computers can outperform classical methods, and now the race is on to make them useful. We build these tools to solve challenging problems in fields ranging from sustainable energy and materials science to drug discovery and financial optimization—problems that demand far more than a single benchmark-beating result. That’s why, at IBM Quantum Developer Conference 2026 (QDC 2026), we’re tracking our progress across the four pathways that carry us from advantage to useful applications: (1) advantage with frontier circuits, (2) the path to IBM Quantum Starling, (3) the path to integrations, and (4) the path to practical applications. Progress across these pathways gets us to our ultimate goal: a quantum computing platform informed by real workflows. Below, we look at each in turn, starting with the foundation: processors built for speed. Advantage with frontier circuits The foundation of a useful quantum supercomputing platform is hardware built for speed, making frontier circuits not just possible, but also cost efficient. This year, we introduced IBM Quantum Nighthawk r2 , our most advanced processor yet, built to run accurate circuits with more than 7,500 quantum operations. Its square-lattice connectivity across 120 programmable qubits (458 physical qubits) allows it to run circuits that are far more challenging for classical methods to simulate. And, as our fastest processor yet, its high-speed qubit reset architecture reaches up to 100,000 samples per second—a 25x throughput gain over IBM Quantum Heron. We’ve already begun using Nighthawk r2 to replicate this year’s advantage demonstrations, and users are putting it to work as well. Run frontier circuits with our hands-on tutorials, which include a 64-qubit ergodicity experiment and a 96-qubit classical shadows analysis. Explore the tutorials: Onset of ergodicity and Classical shadows . In fact, clients and partners including E.ON, Algorithmiq, and Q-CTRL have now run more than 34 billion circuits on Nighthawk r2 according to our team’s calculations, reporting performance improvements of up to 19x beyond previous IBM Quantum processors. The IBM team saw the same pattern in its own research. One simulation experiment studying real magnetic materials run earlier this year with Oak Ridge National Laboratory delivered a 12x speedup, producing outputs consistent with neutron scattering experiments. Meanwhile, an Algorithmiq experiment simulating the quantum dynamics of a heterogeneous material, first demonstrated on IBM Quantum Heron as part of this year's quantum advantage results, now executes 8x faster on Nighthawk r2. Read the full Nighthawk r2 announcement on the IBM Quantum blog. By taking advantage of Nighthawk r2's square-lattice connectivity, the extended Algorithmiq experiment also enables circuits that are significantly more demanding for leading classical tensor-network methods to simulate. At fixed accuracy, those classical methods would require an estimated 240x more memory than for the original heavy-hex implementation, even as the quantum computation itself runs 8x faster.
